description: We are a team of four students bringing together software engineering, astrophysics, and 3D modeling. We share an interest in space exploration and a desire to turn scientific data into useful, engaging experiences.
summary:
Martian Map is a browser-based Mars map that plans a Marswalk and then lets you walk it.

It starts from a 3D globe built from several NASA missions — MOLA and HRSC elevation, Viking colour imagery, CTX and HiRISE imagery, THEMIS day and night infrared, TES thermal inertia, and the USGS geologic map. Between any two points on Mars it runs an A* search in which a step costs not distance but oxygen: suit walking speed and metabolic cost follow the signed slope, ground type comes from TES thermal inertia, and terrain beyond the model's limits is excluded. The result is an EVA budget — oxygen, time, radiation dose, and the point of no return.

You then stand on that same route on HiRISE terrain at one metre per cell, on foot or in a rover, with a helmet display showing slope, consumables, walk-back margin, dose, Mars local time and signal delay to Earth. Mars time follows the NASA GISS Mars24 algorithm and the sky follows the IAU rotation elements, so the Sun and the stars are correct for any place and any moment.

Radiation comes from Curiosity's RAD instrument, space weather from NOAA and NASA DONKI, rover positions from NASA MMGIS. Existing Mars maps answer what is where. This one answers whether you can get there and still breathe on the way back.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Martian Map is a single web application that takes a user from a global view of Mars down to one surface excursion, and prices that excursion in the only currency that matters on an EVA: oxygen.

Route planning. The user picks any two points on Mars — by clicking the globe or typing coordinates. The planner runs an A* search over a gridded elevation model. The cost of moving between two cells is not metres but litres of oxygen: suit walking speed and metabolic cost are derived from the signed slope, so climbing and descending are priced differently; ground type comes from TES thermal inertia, and loose sand nearly doubles the cost of a step; terrain beyond the validated slope range of the model is excluded rather than guessed at. The heuristic is great-circle distance multiplied by the minimum possible cost per metre, which never overestimates the remaining cost, so the search returns an optimal path rather than merely a feasible one. The search runs in a Web Worker, so the interface stays responsive.

The output is an EVA budget: oxygen corridor, time, radiation dose, an elevation profile, a return rule with a 30-minute reserve, and the point of no return — the place on the route past which the remaining consumables no longer cover the walk home. A two-person mode doubles the oxygen while keeping the reserve per person, reflecting the buddy rule for single-failure tolerance.

Science along the way. For any route the application reads the layers beneath it and proposes where it is worth stopping: contacts between geologic units from USGS SIM 3292, rock exposures and sand fields from TES thermal inertia, the steepest scarp where strata are exposed in cross-section, and vantage points on the elevation profile. Each candidate names the layer it came from and that layer's resolution, and can be turned into a routed stop in one click. A separate catalogue of published studies with resolvable DOIs is searched along the corridor of the route and states plainly when nothing is nearby.

First-person traverse. The same route can be walked. Three areas are served on real HiRISE digital terrain models at 1 m per cell with 0.25 m orthoimagery: the boxwork area on Mount Sharp in Gale crater, where Curiosity's real track lies on the terrain; Jezero crater along Perseverance's recent route; and the Ares 3 site in Acidalia Planitia from The Martian. The user walks or drives a rover with a mast camera. A helmet display shows coordinates and elevation, compass bearing to base, slope underfoot and ahead, consumables, time back to base and the point of no return, radiation, Mars local time in both mean and true solar time, Mars Sol Date, the rover's mission sol, and the one-way signal delay to Earth. Walking speed follows the suit model; slopes beyond the limit and areas without data are blocked.

Supporting modes. A flat 2D atlas stacks any layers with independent opacity and reads 1,897 official IAU feature names and the geologic unit under the cursor. Rover routes show Perseverance, Curiosity and Ingenuity traverses and last known positions from NASA MMGIS. A memorial lists every lander and rover that fell silent, with coordinates, dates and one line on what it proved.

HOW IT WORKS

Three layers. A React 18 / TypeScript front end draws the globe, the terrain and the sky with one three.js engine, so a route planned on the globe opens in the first-person mode without any transformation — the same coordinates, a different level of detail. The flat atlas is drawn on Canvas 2D to avoid loading a 3D engine where it is not needed, and rover models are shipped as Draco-compressed glTF.

A Python 3.12 / FastAPI back end serves routes, EVA budgets, coverage answers, the science catalogue and live conditions, with PostgreSQL and PostGIS holding route geometry and the catalogue so that "which published studies lie within the corridor of this route" is an indexed spatial query rather than a scan. External services are fetched through httpx with time-to-live caching: space weather for ten minutes, rover positions for an hour, raw images for a day.

A set of Python pipelines rebuilds the working rasters — slope and ground type — from the primary NASA products rather than storing someone else's derived files. They include WMS and WMTS fetchers, a decoder for the VICAR raster format in which JPL and ASU serve numeric data, GeoTIFF and DTM packing for the browser, Blender scene baking, and JPL Horizons ephemerides. Every raster records the instrument, the resolution and the export date, and that date is shown in the interface.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Existing Mars tools — Mars Trek, JMARS, the PDS archives — are reference systems: they answer what is where, and they do it better than we could. None of them answers the operational question an astronaut actually faces: can I reach that outcrop, and will I still have oxygen to get back. Martian Map adds that layer on top of the same public data.

The immediate benefit is one view instead of five: a user no longer switches between a tile viewer, a geologic map, a rover traverse page and a radiation archive to answer one question. The deeper benefit is that the map is explicit about the limits of its own data: it states where detailed terrain ends, which values are measured and which are modelled, and it returns "no data" rather than yesterday's number when a live service is silent.

The intended impact is twofold. For mission planning and analogue training it is a usable prototype of how multi-mission orbital data can be turned into an EVA consumables decision. For education and outreach it lets a student stand on Mars at a real place, at a real time of day, with real numbers on the visor — which is a far stronger way to learn what 0.38 g, a 24-hour-39-minute sol and an eleven-minute signal delay actually mean than any diagram.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Front end: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, three.js, Web Workers, Canvas 2D, Draco-compressed glTF.

Back end: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Pydantic, PostgreSQL with PostGIS, SQLAlchemy, Alembic, httpx with TTL caching, Gunicorn and Uvicorn.

Data pipelines: NumPy, Pillow, rasterio, WMS and WMTS fetchers, VICAR raster decoding, GeoTIFF and DTM packing, Blender scene baking, JPL Horizons ephemerides.

Delivery: Docker, nginx with a tile cache, Railway, GitHub Actions, pytest, Vitest, ruff, strict TypeScript — 471 automated tests.

CREATIVITY

Three choices set this apart from a layer viewer.

First, the unit of cost. Treating oxygen rather than distance as the edge weight of the search turns a navigation problem into a life-support problem, and it produces routes a real crew would recognise: longer in kilometres, cheaper in breathing.

Second, one engine for the globe and the surface. Because the planner and the walk share a model, they cannot disagree; a class of tests enforces this by requiring the browser's TypeScript to reproduce the Python result to five decimal places, so the build fails if the two ever drift apart.

Third, The Martian route. The demo includes Mark Watney's 3,500 km traverse from Ares 3 in Acidalia Planitia to Ares 4 in Schiaparelli crater, over real MOLA relief, with the HiRISE images taken in 2015 at the coordinates Andy Weir sent to the HiRISE team, and the HiRISE team's own note that the real terrain is far harder than the novel allows. It is the clearest demonstration we found of the difference between a line drawn on an overview map and a walk that the data can actually support.

FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

Resolution honesty: a point is called "detailed" only where a detailed product is genuinely shipped, decided by a registry of served products rather than by a wish list of candidates.

Model validity: the Santee load-carriage model is validated in Earth gravity, and no field data exists for 0.38 g, so the application reports a corridor rather than a single number with false precision.

Measurement location: NOAA space weather is measured near Earth, not at Mars, so it is presented as an advisory signal and never converted into a Martian dose.

Provenance: every layer carries its instrument, resolution, coverage, credit and source link in the product itself, as the Space Apps data rules require.

Accessibility: it runs in a browser on a phone, with render density adapting to the device in real time, and needs no installation or account.
